slides.note: Primary retroperitoneal means the organ formed behind the peritoneum and never had a mesentery. The suprarenal gland sits in its own compartment of renal fascia, so a kidney can be removed for transplant, or can drop (nephroptosis), while the gland stays attached to the diaphragm.

Anterior view, so the patient's left is on your right. Find the left renal vein: it crosses anterior to the aorta, just below the SMA (superior mesenteric artery), to reach the IVC (inferior vena cava). The renal arteries are hidden posterior to the renal veins. Each suprarenal gland sits on the superomedial part (upper, inner corner) of its kidney. Each ureter runs down on psoas major, and the gonadal (testicular) vessels cross in front of it.

Correction: the dashed transpyloric plane belongs at the level of the L1 vertebra; it is drawn about one level too high here, across the T12 label. Posterior view, so the patient's left is on your left. The left kidney sits higher because the liver pushes the right one down (by about 2.5 cm). The transpyloric plane lies near the left hilum, about 5 cm from the midline (the 5 cm arrow), and passes through the superior pole of the right kidney. The 12th rib crosses the upper part of each kidney.

Renal fascia is also called Gerota fascia. Its anterior and posterior layers are closed above and medially, but only loosely joined below. So pus or blood around a kidney can track down into the pelvis. It cannot cross to the other kidney, because medially the fascia blends with the renal vessels at the hilum.

Layers from inside out: fibrous capsule → perirenal (perinephric) fat → renal fascia → pararenal (paranephric) fat → transversalis fascia. Don't confuse them: perirenal fat is inside the fascia, hugging the kidney; pararenal fat is outside it, mostly behind.

Cross-section seen from below, as on a CT scan, with the front of the body at the top. Follow the renal fascia (purple line): its anterior and posterior layers wrap the kidney and perinephric fat, and paranephric fat lies outside, behind. The kidney rests on psoas major medially and quadratus lumborum posteriorly, so its hilum faces anteromedially (forward and toward the vertebra).

Section at L2 seen from below, so the patient's right is on your left. Find the left renal vein passing between the SMA in front and the aorta behind on its way to the IVC; this is where it gets squeezed in nutcracker syndrome. The duodenum and right colic flexure lie directly in front of the right kidney.

(A) The lumbar approach to the kidney: the surgeon enters from the back, between the back muscles and the flat abdominal muscles, then opens the renal fascia and perinephric fat. The subcostal nerve (T12) and the L1 anterior ramus (iliohypogastric and ilio-inguinal nerves) run diagonally across the back of the kidney, so they are at risk here.

Simple rule: the glomeruli and the coiled (convoluted) tubules sit in the cortex. The straight parts sit in the medulla: the straight parts of the proximal and distal tubules, the loops of Henle and the last stretch of each collecting duct. "Proximal" collecting duct means its first part (in the cortex); "distal" collecting duct means its last part (in the medulla).

Follow the urine: renal papilla (tip of a pyramid) → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter. Renal columns are cortex reaching inward between the pyramids, toward the renal sinus; the interlobar vessels run in them. Fat in the renal sinus surrounds the pelvis and calyces.

A nephron = renal corpuscle (glomerulus inside Bowman's capsule) + tubule: proximal tubule → loop of Henle → distal tubule, which empties into a collecting duct. In (c), red = blood coming in from the renal artery, blue = blood going out to the renal vein, and small arrows show the direction of flow. The afferent arteriole carries blood into the glomerulus. The efferent arteriole carries it out and forms a second capillary bed around the tubules (peritubular capillaries) before blood returns to the renal vein.

Follow the colors: blue = proximal tubule, white = thin limbs of the loop, orange = distal tubule (thick ascending limb + distal convoluted tubule), gray = collecting duct, which opens on the papilla. Juxtamedullary nephrons (corpuscle next to the medulla) have long loops reaching deep into the inner medulla; cortical nephrons have short loops. The macula densa (black) is where the distal tubule touches its own glomerulus.

Each colored patch is where that structure touches the kidney. On the right kidney the liver covers most of the front, and the duodenum lies over the hilum. Behind, only the 12th rib crosses the right kidney; the higher left kidney is crossed by both the 11th and 12th ribs. Below the ribs the kidney rests on psoas major, quadratus lumborum and transversus abdominis, from medial to lateral (in the posterior view, medial is on your left).

Use the left kidney in both drawings. Front view (left kidney on your right): the suprarenal gland caps the medial side of the upper pole; the stomach and spleen cover the rest of it; the pancreas crosses the middle; the left colic flexure and descending colon lie on the lower lateral half; the jejunum lies on the lower medial half. Back view (left kidney on your left): the diaphragm and both the 11th and 12th ribs lie over the upper part; below them lie psoas major, quadratus lumborum and transversus abdominis, from medial to lateral.

pic.src: Gray's Anatomy for Students 3e, Fig. 4.138 (similar figure)
Gray's Anatomy for Students 3e, Fig. 4.139 (similar figure)

slides.note: The black arrow passes through the omental (epiploic) foramen, the opening into the lesser sac; the right suprarenal gland lies at the same level. Each shaded "Contacts …" area shows which organ touches that part of the kidney.

Also called Morison pouch. When a patient lies on the back, it is a low, gravity-dependent spot of the upper abdomen, so free fluid such as blood (hemoperitoneum) pools here early. It is one of the first places checked on bedside trauma ultrasound.

Side view of a patient lying on the back, head on your left. Fluid poured into the abdomen runs to the two lowest spots: the hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch, the upper one, under the liver) and the rectovesical pouch (rectouterine pouch in a woman, the lower one, in the pelvis). The black arrow shows fluid from the lesser sac (omental bursa) draining into the hepatorenal recess.

The renal arteries leave the aorta at the L1–L2 disc, just below the SMA. The right renal artery is longer, because the aorta lies left of the midline; on its way to the kidney it passes posterior to the IVC. Segmental arteries are end arteries (no connections between them), so blocking one kills its whole segment, and each segment can be removed surgically on its own.

Correction: the interlobar arteries are missing; they come right before the arcuate arteries. Full order: renal → segmental → lobar → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular (cortical radiate) → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries / vasa recta (straight capillaries running beside the loops of Henle).

Anterior view, so the patient's right is on your left. Find the right renal artery passing posterior to the IVC, and the long left renal vein crossing anterior to the aorta just below the SMA. Each suprarenal gland gets three arteries: superior (from the inferior phrenic artery), middle (from the aorta) and inferior (from the renal artery).

Five segments, each with its own artery. The anterior branch of the renal artery supplies four: superior, anterior superior, anterior inferior and inferior. The posterior branch supplies only the posterior segment. The superior and inferior segments wrap around the poles, so they show on both surfaces.

Where each artery runs: interlobar arteries run outward from the renal sinus between the pyramids (in the renal columns); arcuate arteries arch over the pyramid bases at the cortex–medulla border; cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries run outward through the cortex toward the capsule and give off the afferent arterioles. The renal artery splits into anterior and posterior branches before the hilum.

Anterior view, so the left kidney is on your right. Find the accessory renal artery: an extra artery that leaves the aorta below the main left renal artery and runs up to the lower part of the left kidney's hilum. Extra renal arteries (about 30% of people) are embryonic vessels that did not regress as the kidney rose. They are end arteries, so tying one off kills that part of the kidney, and a lower-pole artery can cross and obstruct the ureter.

Anterior view, so the patient's right is on your left. The IVC has been cut and its upper part lifted, to show the arteries that pass posterior to it, such as the right renal artery. The renal veins are cut too, so the kidneys could be pulled aside. Inset: the suprarenal gland is two glands in one, an outer cortex around an inner medulla.

Don't confuse the sides: on the right, the suprarenal and gonadal veins drain straight into the IVC; only on the left do they drain into the renal vein. So a blocked left renal vein (nutcracker, a left kidney tumor growing into the vein) backs blood into the left testicular vein and can cause a left varicocele. Nutcracker syndrome and renal vein entrapment syndrome are the same thing.

Lateral view from the left: the front of the body is on your left, and the aorta lies at the back. The SMA leaves the aorta at a sharp angle. The left renal vein (blue circle; the ring on the aorta is the left renal artery) and, just below it, the 3rd part of the duodenum pass through that angle. If the angle narrows, the SMA squeezes the vein against the aorta like a nutcracker.

Correction: in NCS (nutcracker syndrome), nausea and vomiting come from squeezing of the 3rd part of the duodenum in the same SMA–aorta angle, not from splanchnic veins. The rest comes from back-pressure in the left renal vein: swollen veins in the kidney leak blood into the urine (hematuria; over time, anemia). The left gonadal vein drains into the renal vein, so men get left testicular pain and women left lower quadrant (ovarian vein) pain.

Sympathetic fibers come mainly from the least splanchnic nerve (T12), relay in the aorticorenal ganglion and reach the kidney along the renal artery; they constrict the afferent and efferent arterioles. Parasympathetic fibers come from the vagus. Pain fibers run back with the sympathetic fibers to T10–L1, so kidney pain is felt in the flank and low back.

Follow each ureter down. It lies on the psoas major and passes posterior to the testicular (gonadal) vessels. It enters the pelvis by crossing the external iliac artery just past the common iliac bifurcation. Near the bladder, the ductus deferens crosses superior to it; nothing else lies between the ureter and the peritoneum there.

Superior view (looking down into the pelvis, front at the top), so the patient's right is on your right. On that side the peritoneum is removed: find where the ureter passes inferior to the uterine artery beside the cervix, "water under the bridge." When a surgeon ties the uterine artery in a hysterectomy (removal of the uterus), the ureter can be clamped or cut here. The ovarian vessels also lie close to the ureter at the pelvic brim, a second injury point.

Anterior view, so the patient's right is on your left. Find the three normal narrowings of each ureter, where stones get stuck: (1) the ureteropelvic junction, where the renal pelvis becomes the ureter; (2) the pelvic inlet (pelvic brim), where the ureter crosses anterior to the end of the common iliac artery or the start of the external iliac artery; (3) the entrance to the bladder, where it passes through the bladder wall.

pic.src: Gray's Anatomy for Students 3e, Fig. 4.143 (similar figure)

slides.note: A pyelogram is an X-ray taken after contrast dye fills the renal pelvis and ureters (here pushed up from the bladder through a catheter). Red 1–3 = the three normal narrowings: (1) ureteropelvic junction, (2) crossing of the external iliac artery at the pelvic brim, (3) passage through the bladder wall. Black arrows = renal papillae bulging into minor calices.

The abdominal ureter gets small branches from the renal (most constant), gonadal (testicular or ovarian), aorta and common iliac arteries. The pelvic ureter gets branches from the internal iliac system (superior and inferior vesical; uterine in females). The ascending and descending twigs join into one thin chain along the ureter wall, so stripping the ureter in surgery (peeling off its outer sheath, where this chain runs) can starve it of blood.

Find the "ureteric branch" labels top to bottom: renal → aorta → ovarian and common iliac → inferior vesical → superior vesical. Each supplies the stretch of ureter nearest to it. In the abdomen the branches reach the ureter from its medial side; in the pelvis, from its lateral side.

Anterior view, so the patient's left kidney is on your right. Find the accessory renal artery there: an extra artery from the aorta to the lower part of the left kidney, left over from the kidney's embryonic ascent. A lower-pole artery can cross anterior to the ureter and block it. At the bottom, branches of the superior vesical arteries run up to the lower ureter.

Lymph follows the veins. Kidney and upper ureter drain to the lumbar nodes: caval nodes beside the IVC (inferior vena cava) and aortic nodes beside the aorta. Middle ureter → common iliac nodes. Lower (pelvic) ureter → common, external or internal iliac nodes.

Inset: inside the kidney, lymph vessels run beside the arteries (interlobular → arcuate → interlobar) and leave at the hilum (arrows show flow). Main picture: they reach the lateral aortic (lumbar) nodes, then the lumbar trunks carry lymph up to the cisterna chyli (the sac where the thoracic duct begins).

The plexuses are the renal, abdominal aortic and superior hypogastric plexuses. Pain fibers from a stretched ureter run back with the sympathetic nerves to cord segments T11–L2. The brain reads the pain as coming from the skin those segments supply, so it is felt on the same side from the loin to the groin.

Key: yellow = sympathetic nerves, green = parasympathetic nerves (vagus), purple = plexuses that carry both. The renal nerve plexus (purple, around the renal artery) carries sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers into the kidney and down the upper ureter. Its sympathetic input comes mainly from the least splanchnic nerve, which synapses in the aorticorenal ganglion. Its parasympathetic input comes from the vagus (posterior vagal trunk).

Red = sympathetic, blue = parasympathetic, black = pain (afferent) fibers; solid = preganglionic, dashed = postganglionic. Sympathetic fibers leave cord segments T10–L1 in the lesser, least and 1st lumbar splanchnic nerves and synapse in the aorticorenal and renal ganglia. Pain fibers run the same path back (kidney T10–L1; ureter down to L2). Parasympathetic: vagus to the kidney; pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) to the lower ureter.

A staghorn stone fills the renal pelvis and branches into the calices like a deer antler. It is usually made of struvite and forms in infections with urease-making bacteria such as Proteus. Small loose stones in the pelvis are the ones that drop into the ureter and cause colic.

Colic pain moves with the stone, from loin to groin: flank first, then the inguinal region, then the scrotum or labia and front of the thigh (genitofemoral nerve, L1–L2). The X-rays and green arrows show stones stuck at the three narrowings. Pararenal pain: the kidney lies on the psoas major, a hip flexor, so extending the hip stretches the psoas and worsens pain from inflammation around the kidney.

Pus around the kidney stays inside the renal fascia. At the hilum the fascia is fixed to the renal vessels and ureter, so pus does not cross to the other kidney. Below, the front and back layers are only loosely joined, so pus can track down into the pelvis. Causes: an ascending urinary tract infection, spread through the blood (often Staph aureus), diabetes, and stones or cysts that block urine flow.

Anterior view, so the patient's right is on your left. Find both suprarenal glands on top of the kidneys. The right one lies posterior to the IVC ("I. Vena Cava"). The left one lies beside the aorta, next to the celiac trunk and its ganglion. Between the two glands, from the patient's right to left (your left to right): IVC, right crus, celiac ganglion, celiac trunk, SMA (superior mesenteric artery), left crus. The crura (the diaphragm's two muscular legs beside the aorta) are not labeled here.

Why it matters: the thin septum gives the gland its own compartment, firmly attached to the diaphragm. So when a loose kidney drops (nephroptosis), the gland stays put. A donor kidney can also be removed without damaging the gland.

Sagittal section seen from the right: the front (liver, colon) is on your right, the back muscles on your left. Follow the layers from the kidney outward: fibrous capsule → perirenal fat → renal (Gerota's) fascia → pararenal fat. The suprarenal gland sits above the kidney, inside the same fascia, just under the diaphragm. The fascia's two layers are open at the bottom, which is why pus can track down.

Right gland: lies anterolateral to the right crus; the IVC touches the gland's anteromedial side and the liver its anterolateral side. Left gland: lies medial to the upper half of the left kidney, posterior to the stomach and pancreas, near the spleen.

Examples: glucocorticoid = cortisol; mineralocorticoid = aldosterone. Aldosterone makes the kidney keep Na⁺ and water, which is how the cortex holds up blood volume and blood pressure (BP). Veins and lymph leave at the hilum, but arteries and nerves enter all over the surface.

Three arteries, each from the nearest big artery: superior from the inferior phrenic (above), middle from the aorta near the SMA (beside), inferior from the renal (below). They split into 50–60 twigs over the whole surface. One vein, asymmetric: the right is short and enters the IVC directly; the left is longer and drains into the left renal vein.

Upper-left panel (right gland). Find the short right suprarenal vein running straight into the IVC (retracted medially here). Because it is so short, it is easy to tear when the right gland is removed. Note the arteries from three sources entering from above, medially and below. Inset (lower left): the gland is an outer cortex around an inner medulla.
Lower-right panel (left gland). Find the longer left suprarenal vein running down to the left renal vein. The pancreas and spleen lie anterior to this gland (here lifted up).

A sympathetic path normally has two neurons with a synapse in a ganglion. Here the presynaptic fibers, from the lateral horn (IML, intermediolateral cell column) of cord segments T10–L1, pass through the sympathetic trunk (paravertebral) and celiac (prevertebral) ganglia without synapsing. They end directly on the chromaffin cells, which act as the second neuron but release epinephrine into the blood.

Solid lines = preganglionic (presynaptic) fibers; dashed = postganglionic (postsynaptic) fibers. Fibers for the medulla cells pass the celiac ganglion without synapsing. Fibers for the gland's blood vessels synapse in the celiac ganglion first; dashed postganglionic fibers then run on to the vessels. The drawing shows only roots T5–T8 of the greater splanchnic nerve; the main supply comes from segments T10–L1.

A tumor of the chromaffin cells. It releases bursts of epinephrine and norepinephrine, so symptoms come in episodes: high BP, headache, sweating and a pounding heart (palpitations). Lab clue: high metanephrines (catecholamine breakdown products) in plasma or urine.

(A) Bifid pelvis: the renal pelvis splits in two because the ureteric bud divided partly. (B) Bifid ureter: two ureters join before the bladder (one opening); duplicated ureter: two separate openings into the bladder (uncommon). (C) Retrocaval ureter: the right ureter passes posterior to the IVC and can be compressed. (D) Horseshoe kidney: lower poles fuse; it stays at L3–L5 because the IMA (inferior mesenteric artery) blocks its ascent. (E) Ectopic pelvic kidney: never ascended; fed by anomalous renal vessels from the aortic bifurcation or common iliac artery. Don't mistake it for a pelvic tumor.

pic.src: Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7e, Fig. B2.32

qs.q: The kidneys, ureters and suprarenal glands are what type of structure?
qs.why: They form behind the peritoneum and never have a mesentery, which is what 'primary' means; secondarily retroperitoneal organs once had a mesentery.

qs.q: At which vertebral levels do the kidneys lie on the posterior abdominal wall?
qs.why: Each kidney spans about T12 to L3, with its upper part lying deep to the lower ribs.

qs.q: Which kidney lies higher, and why?
opts: Left, because the liver pushes the right down
Left, because the aorta lies left of midline
Right, because the IVC lies on the right
Right, because the spleen pushes the left down
qs.why: The large liver sits above the right kidney and pushes it down by about 2.5 cm, so the left kidney is higher.

qs.q: The transpyloric plane (L1) passes through which part of the left kidney?
qs.why: L1 passes through the left hilum; on the lower right kidney it passes through the superior pole.

qs.q: Moving outward from the kidney, what is the order of the layers?
opts: Capsule, renal fascia, perirenal fat, pararenal fat
Capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, pararenal fat
Renal fascia, capsule, perirenal fat, pararenal fat
Capsule, pararenal fat, renal fascia, perirenal fat
qs.why: Perirenal fat lies inside the renal (Gerota) fascia hugging the kidney; pararenal fat lies outside the fascia, mostly behind.

qs.q: Where are the anterior and posterior layers of renal fascia only loosely joined?
opts: Nowhere; they are fused all around
qs.why: The layers are closed above (diaphragm fascia) and medially (renal vessels) but loosely joined below, so fluid around the kidney can track down into the pelvis.

qs.q: The kidney rests on psoas major medially and quadratus lumborum behind. Which way does its hilum face?
qs.why: Lying on the sloping psoas and quadratus lumborum tilts the kidney so its hilum faces anteromedially.

qs.q: In the posterior (lumbar) surgical approach to the kidney, which nerves are at risk?
opts: Genitofemoral and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves
qs.why: The subcostal nerve (T12) and the L1 anterior ramus (iliohypogastric and ilio-inguinal nerves) run diagonally across the back of the kidney.

qs.q: From anterior to posterior, what is the order of structures at the renal hilum?
qs.why: The renal vein is most anterior, the artery lies behind it, and the renal pelvis is most posterior.

qs.q: What is the space inside the kidney that the hilum opens into?
qs.why: The hilum is the entrance to the renal sinus, the space that holds the renal pelvis, calices and vessels.

qs.q: Each minor calyx encircles which structure?
qs.why: The renal papilla (apex of a pyramid) pokes into a minor calyx; 2–3 minor calices join to form a major calyx.

qs.q: Which structures lie in the renal cortex?
qs.why: Glomeruli and the coiled tubules sit in the cortex; the straight parts (loops of Henle, medullary collecting ducts) run down into the medulla.

qs.q: What are renal columns?
opts: Cortex extending inward between the pyramids
Folds of the renal pelvis wall
Medulla extending outward into the cortex
qs.why: Renal columns are cortical tissue reaching inward between the medullary pyramids, toward the renal sinus; the interlobar vessels run in them.

qs.q: Which nephrons have long loops of Henle reaching deep into the inner medulla?
qs.why: Juxtamedullary nephrons have their corpuscle next to the medulla and long loops; cortical nephrons have short loops.

qs.q: Where is the macula densa?
opts: Where the collecting duct opens on the papilla
Where the proximal tubule leaves Bowman's capsule
Where the distal tubule touches its own glomerulus
At the hairpin tip of the loop of Henle
qs.why: The macula densa is the patch of distal tubule that returns to touch its own glomerulus.

qs.q: Which structure lies directly anterior to the hilum of the right kidney?
qs.why: The duodenum lies over the right renal hilum, while the liver covers most of the rest of the anterior surface.

qs.q: Which organ contacts the anterior surface of the left kidney but not the right?
qs.why: Stomach, spleen, pancreas, jejunum and descending colon lie in front of the left kidney; liver, duodenum and ascending colon lie in front of the right.

qs.q: Which ribs cross the posterior surface of the left kidney?
qs.why: The left kidney sits higher, so both the 11th and 12th ribs cross it; only the 12th rib crosses the lower right kidney.

qs.q: Below the ribs, which muscles lie behind the kidney, from medial to lateral?
opts: Psoas major, quadratus lumborum, transversus abdominis
Transversus abdominis, quadratus lumborum, psoas major
Psoas major, transversus abdominis, quadratus lumborum
Quadratus lumborum, psoas major, transversus abdominis
qs.why: Psoas major lies medially beside the spine, quadratus lumborum in the middle, and transversus abdominis laterally.

qs.q: The hepatorenal recess separates which two structures?
qs.why: It is the space between the liver and the right kidney; the space between the liver and diaphragm is the subphrenic recess.

qs.q: Why does free blood collect early in the hepatorenal recess?
opts: It opens directly into the lesser sac
It is the lowest upper-abdominal space when supine
It connects with the pleural cavity
qs.why: In a patient lying on the back, the hepatorenal (Morison) recess is gravity-dependent, so blood pools there early and it is checked first on trauma ultrasound.

qs.q: Under normal conditions, what does the hepatorenal recess contain?
opts: Nothing; it is a potential space
qs.why: It is a potential space that fills only when fluid, such as blood in hemoperitoneum, collects in the abdomen.

qs.q: Why is the right renal artery longer than the left?
opts: It arises from the SMA instead
The aorta lies left of the midline
It must loop around the duodenum
qs.why: The aorta sits slightly to the left, so the right renal artery travels farther, passing posterior to the IVC.

qs.q: Why does blocking one segmental renal artery infarct its whole segment?
opts: Segments get blood only from capsular arteries
Segmental arteries anastomose freely with each other
Segmental arteries are end arteries without anastomoses
qs.why: Segmental arteries have no connections with each other, so each segment depends on its own artery and can also be removed surgically on its own.

qs.q: How are the five segmental arteries of each kidney arranged?
opts: Two superior, two inferior, one posterior
qs.why: The anterior branch gives four segmental arteries (superior, anterosuperior, anteroinferior, inferior); the posterior branch gives one.

qs.q: In the renal arterial tree, which arteries come directly before the arcuate arteries?
qs.why: Order: segmental → lobar → interlobar (in the renal columns) → arcuate (over the pyramid bases) → interlobular → afferent arteriole.

qs.q: In nutcracker syndrome, the left renal vein is squeezed between which two structures?
opts: Celiac trunk in front and aorta behind
SMA in front and aorta behind
SMA in front and IVC behind
Aorta in front and vertebra behind
qs.why: The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta just below the SMA, so a narrow SMA–aorta angle compresses it.

qs.q: Why can a blocked left renal vein cause a left varicocele?
opts: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein
The left testicular vein drains straight into the IVC
The left renal vein drains into the testicular vein
The left testicular artery arises from the left renal artery
qs.why: Only on the left do the gonadal and suprarenal veins drain into the renal vein; on the right they enter the IVC directly.

qs.q: In nutcracker syndrome, what causes the nausea and vomiting?
opts: Compression of the 3rd part of the duodenum
Back-pressure in the left renal vein
qs.why: The 3rd part of the duodenum passes through the same SMA–aorta angle just below the left renal vein, so it is squeezed too; the splanchnic veins are not involved.

qs.q: Pain fibers from the kidney return with sympathetic fibers to which spinal cord segments?
qs.why: Kidney pain travels back along the sympathetic route to T10–L1, so it is felt in the flank and low back.

qs.q: On psoas major, how does the ureter relate to the gonadal vessels?
opts: It runs medial to them, never crossing
It runs lateral to them, never crossing
qs.why: The testicular or ovarian vessels cross in front of the ureter as it descends on psoas major.

qs.q: During a hysterectomy, where is the ureter at risk of being clamped?
opts: Passing inferior to the round ligament
Passing through the deep inguinal ring
Passing inferior to the uterine artery beside the cervix
Passing superior to the uterine artery near the fundus
qs.why: 'Water under the bridge': the ureter runs under the uterine artery beside the cervix, so tying the artery can catch it.

qs.q: Which is one of the three normal narrowings where ureteric stones lodge?
opts: Midpoint of its course on psoas major
Crossing of the external iliac artery at the pelvic brim
qs.why: The three narrowings are the ureteropelvic junction, the crossing of the external iliac artery at the pelvic brim, and the passage through the bladder wall.

qs.q: In males, which structure crosses superior to the ureter near the bladder?
qs.why: Near the bladder the ductus deferens crosses over the ureter; nothing else lies between the ureter and the peritoneum there.

qs.q: The pelvic part of the ureter gets its arteries mainly from which source?
opts: Branches of the inferior mesenteric artery
Branches of the external iliac artery
Branches of the internal iliac artery
qs.why: The pelvic ureter gets superior and inferior vesical (and, in females, uterine) branches of the internal iliac; the abdominal ureter gets renal, gonadal, aortic and common iliac branches.

qs.q: A lower-pole accessory renal artery can cause which problem?
opts: Compression of the left renal vein
qs.why: An extra artery to the lower pole, left over from the kidney's ascent, can cross anterior to the ureter and block it.

qs.q: Lymph from the kidney drains first to which nodes?
qs.why: Kidney lymph follows the renal veins to the lumbar nodes beside the IVC and aorta.

qs.q: Lymph from the middle part of the ureter drains to which nodes?
qs.why: Upper ureter → lumbar nodes; middle ureter → common iliac nodes; lower ureter → common, external or internal iliac nodes.

qs.q: Pain fibers from the ureter travel with sympathetic fibers to which cord segments?
qs.why: Ureteric pain enters T11–L2, so it is referred to the same-side skin from loin to groin.

qs.q: A staghorn stone filling the renal pelvis is usually made of what?
qs.why: Staghorn stones are usually struvite, formed in infections with urease-making bacteria such as Proteus.

qs.q: Why does extending the hip worsen pain from inflammation around the kidney?
opts: It compresses the renal vein against the aorta
It stretches quadratus lumborum, anterior to the kidney
It stretches the ureter over the pelvic brim
It stretches psoas major, which the kidney lies on
qs.why: The kidney lies on psoas major, a hip flexor, so hip extension stretches the psoas and irritates the inflamed tissue around the kidney.

qs.q: Why does a perinephric abscess not spread to the opposite kidney?
opts: Psoas fascia blocks spread across the spine
Renal fascia is open medially but closed below
Perirenal fat is absent near the midline
Renal fascia is fixed to the hilar vessels medially
qs.why: At the hilum the renal fascia blends with the renal vessels and ureter, sealing it medially; below, the layers are loosely joined, so pus tracks down into the pelvis instead.

qs.q: What shapes are the two suprarenal glands?
qs.why: The right gland is triangular (pyramidal); the left is semilunar (crescent-shaped).

qs.q: The right suprarenal gland lies posterior to which vessel?
qs.why: The right gland tucks behind the IVC against the right crus; the left lies beside the aorta near the celiac trunk.

qs.q: Why does the suprarenal gland stay put when a loose kidney drops (nephroptosis)?
opts: It lies outside the renal fascia entirely
A fascial septum separates it and anchors it to the diaphragm
It is fused to the kidney's fibrous capsule
Its arteries tie it to the aorta
qs.why: A thin septum of renal fascia gives the gland its own compartment, attached to the diaphragmatic crura, so the kidney can move or be removed without it.

qs.q: Which organs lie anterior to the left suprarenal gland?
qs.why: The left gland lies posterior to the stomach and pancreas, near the spleen; the liver and IVC relate to the right gland.

qs.q: From which embryonic tissue does the suprarenal medulla develop?
qs.why: The medulla comes from neural crest cells; the cortex comes from mesoderm.

qs.q: Which suprarenal hormone maintains blood volume by making the kidney keep Na⁺ and water?
qs.why: Aldosterone, a mineralocorticoid from the cortex, makes the kidney retain Na⁺ and water, holding up blood volume and BP.

qs.q: The superior suprarenal arteries arise from which artery?
qs.why: Superior from the inferior phrenic, middle from the aorta, inferior from the renal artery: each from the nearest big artery.

qs.q: Why is the right suprarenal vein easy to tear when removing the right gland?
opts: It runs between the SMA and aorta
It is very short and enters the IVC directly
It drains into the right renal vein
It is long and loops under the renal artery
qs.why: The right vein is short and enters the IVC directly; the left is longer and drains into the left renal vein.

qs.q: Where do presynaptic sympathetic fibers to the suprarenal medulla synapse?
qs.why: They pass through the trunk and celiac ganglia without synapsing; the chromaffin cells act as the second neuron but release epinephrine into the blood.

qs.q: Pheochromocytoma arises from which cells, and what does it secrete?
opts: Medullary chromaffin cells; epinephrine and norepinephrine
qs.why: It is a usually benign tumor of the medulla's chromaffin cells that releases bursts of catecholamines: episodic high BP, headache, sweating, palpitations.

qs.q: Which artery stops a horseshoe kidney from ascending?
qs.why: The fused lower poles catch under the IMA, so a horseshoe kidney stays at about L3–L5.

qs.q: In a retrocaval ureter, which ureter passes behind which vessel?
opts: Left ureter, behind the left renal vein
qs.why: The right ureter passes posterior to the IVC, where it can be compressed.

slides.note: In the drawing (cross-section through the left kidney), the kidney sits in the gutter lateral to psoas major and anterior to quadratus lumborum, wrapped in perirenal fat and renal fascia. On the CT the patient's right is on your left (liver side): both kidneys sit in the gutters beside the vertebral body, with the round aorta just in front of the vertebra and the IVC (inferior vena cava) on the patient's right of it (your left).

Branches leave in three directions. Front (anterior/midline): unpaired arteries to the gut: celiac trunk (T12), SMA (superior mesenteric artery, L1), IMA (inferior mesenteric artery, L3). Sides (lateral): paired arteries to the urogenital and endocrine organs (suprarenal, renal at the L1–L2 disc, gonadal at L2). Back-sides (posterolateral): paired arteries to the diaphragm and body wall (subcostal, inferior phrenic, lumbar).

Find the left renal vein: it crosses anterior to the aorta, just below the SMA, to reach the IVC. There it lies between the SMA in front and the aorta behind, and the two can squeeze it (nutcracker syndrome). Blood then backs up into the left kidney, causing blood in the urine. Because the left gonadal (testicular) and left suprarenal veins drain into the left renal vein, the back-up also swells the veins around the left testis: a left varicocele.

Correction: the lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior rami of L1–L4 (often with a twig from T12). L5 joins part of L4 as the lumbosacral trunk, which belongs to the sacral plexus. On your left (the patient's right) psoas has been removed to show the plexus. The plexus forms inside psoas major, so all 7 branches come out around that muscle: iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh, femoral, obturator, lumbosacral trunk.

Roots are on the right, nerves on the left. L1: iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal. L1–L2: genitofemoral. L2–L3: lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh. L2–L4: femoral and obturator. The bottom labels give direction: every nerve heads lateral except the obturator, which leaves the medial border of psoas. Cremasteric reflex: stroking the upper inner thigh makes the cremaster lift the testis.

On your left (the patient's right) psoas has been removed; on your right it is intact. Nerves around psoas major:
  • Lateral border: iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal (across quadratus lumborum, the unlabeled muscle lateral to psoas); lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh (across iliacus to just medial to the ASIS, anterior superior iliac spine); femoral (in the groove between psoas and iliacus).
  • Anterior surface: genitofemoral, the only one that pierces psoas; it splits into genital and femoral branches (not drawn here) above the inguinal ligament.
  • Medial border: obturator and lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5), both heading into the true pelvis.

pic.src: Gray's Anatomy for Students 3e, Fig. 4.161 (similar figure)

slides.note: The sympathetic trunk (labeled, beside the lower lumbar vertebrae) lies in the groove between the vertebral bodies and the medial edge of psoas; the IVC covers the right trunk and the aorta overlaps the left. Its ganglia send postganglionic fibers through the gray rami communicantes (labeled) back into the spinal nerves, which carry them to vessels and sweat glands of the wall and leg. Its lumbar splanchnic nerves carry preganglionic fibers that synapse in small ganglia of the plexuses around the aorta; postganglionic fibers from there reach the pelvic organs.

Psoas abscess: an infection, classically TB (tuberculosis) of the lumbar spine, spreads into the psoas sheath. Pus runs down this tube, deep to the inguinal ligament, and bulges in the upper thigh; lumbar plexus nerves in the muscle can be irritated. Psoas sign: the patient lies on the healthy side and the examiner pulls the upper (affected-side) thigh backward, extending it (arrow). This stretches psoas, so an inflamed organ lying on it (right side: appendix) hurts. Inset (lower right): the inflamed appendix lies on psoas (P), below the cecum, next to iliacus.

An AAA (abdominal aortic aneurysm) is a bulge where the aortic wall is weak; a large one is felt as a pulsing mass just left of the midline (the patient's left). The severe abdomen or back pain and the ~90% death rate belong to a rupture that is not recognized. Drawing C shows the normal aorta: in thin people it can be pressed against the L4 vertebral body at the level of the umbilicus to slow bleeding in the pelvis or legs.

Right hip bone seen from the outside (lateral view). Its three bones are color-coded: ilium (tan, the upper wing), ischium (blue, lower back) and pubis (pink, lower front). All three meet in the acetabulum, the hip socket (its grey C-shaped joint surface). In children a Y-shaped (triradiate) cartilage joins them there; they fuse into one bone after puberty, by about 16–18 years.

pic.src: Gray's Anatomy for Students 3e, Fig. 5.20 (similar figure)

slides.note: The boxed labels on this and the next bone slides are the landmarks to know for that bone. The ASIS anchors the lateral end of the inguinal ligament. The PSIS (posterior superior iliac spine) lies under the skin dimples of the low back. The greater sciatic notch becomes the greater sciatic foramen once the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments close it.

The pudendal nerve (S2–S4) is the main sensory nerve of the perineum. It hooks around the ischial spine where the sacrospinous ligament attaches, so a finger in the vagina feels the spine and the needle goes just there. This numbs most of the perineum in childbirth. The front of the perineum is supplied by the ilioinguinal nerve (L1), which needs its own block (top label). The side of the perineum gets the perineal branch of the posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh (also labeled).

The linea terminalis is the ridge on the inner hip bone: arcuate line (ilium) + pecten pubis + pubic crest. With the sacral promontory and sacral ala it forms the pelvic brim, which divides the false pelvis above from the true pelvis below.

R marks the patient's right (on your left). Sacrum: midline wedge below L5, meeting each ilium at the sacroiliac joint lines. Iliac ala: the wide wing; iliac crest: its top edge. ASIS: the bump on the wing's outer edge below the crest; AIIS (anterior inferior iliac spine): lower, above the hip joint. Obturator foramen: dark oval low on each side; its upper rim is the superior pubic ramus, its lower rim the ischiopubic ramus. Ischium: bone below and lateral to the foramen. Pubic symphysis: midline gap between the pubic bones.

A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint: bones held by ligament, here the strong interosseous sacroiliac ligament, so the sacroiliac joint barely moves. A secondary cartilaginous joint joins bones with a fibrocartilage pad (pubic symphysis, sacrococcygeal joint, IV = intervertebral disc joint). Zygapophysial joints are the small synovial facet joints between vertebral arches.

Don't confuse: sacrospinous runs from the sacrum to the ischial spine; sacrotuberous runs from the sacrum to the ischial tuberosity. Together they turn the sciatic notches into foramina: the greater sciatic foramen lies above the sacrospinous ligament, the lesser one between the two ligaments. They also keep the lower end of the sacrum from swinging up and back when body weight pushes its top down.

Front view of the pelvis: drawing on the left, X-ray (B) on the right; each label points to the same spot on both. Red line = pelvic inlet, which follows the pelvic brim. Green dashed line = pelvic outlet, the lower opening. The curved double arrow marks the pubic arch under the pubic symphysis. Ilium, ischium and pubis (starred) together form the right hip bone.

Left: the brim (edge of the inlet), part by part: sacral promontory (orange), margin of the sacral ala (green), then the linea terminalis = arcuate line (red) + pecten pubis (blue) + pubic crest (purple), meeting at the top of the pubic symphysis. Right, seen from below: the outlet (green) is diamond-shaped, with the pubic arch in front, the ischial tuberosities at the sides, and the sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx behind.

The pelvic brim (arrows) is the dividing line. Above it, the false (greater) pelvis (pink) is really the lowest part of the abdomen, between the iliac wings. Below it, the true (lesser) pelvis (blue) reaches down to the pelvic diaphragm (levator ani). Under the pelvic diaphragm lies the perineum (orange).

Hand test for the subpubic angle (the angle under the pubic symphysis): a male angle (pink) fits between the spread index and middle fingers; a female angle (green) fits between the spread thumb and index finger. The wider female angle and outlet make room for the baby's head.
The ischial spines sit closer together in males, which is a main reason the male outlet is smaller. Most female features (oval inlet, wide pubic arch, large outlet) make the birth canal wider.

What uses each exit:
  • Deep to the inguinal ligament (drawn here): iliopsoas (psoas major + iliacus, to the lesser trochanter), femoral nerve, artery and vein → front of thigh.
  • Obturator canal: obturator nerve and vessels → medial thigh.
  • Greater sciatic foramen: piriformis, sciatic nerve, gluteal vessels and nerves, pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels → buttock and back of thigh.
  • Lesser sciatic foramen: the pudendal nerve and vessels pass from the buttock into the perineum; the obturator internus tendon passes out to the buttock.
  • Pelvic outlet: urethra, vagina and anal canal → perineum.

The pelvis is a ring, so it usually breaks in two places. A front-to-back crush (car crash) snaps the pubic rami and can tear the bladder or urethra behind them. A fall onto the feet can drive the femoral head through the acetabulum into the pelvis, injuring the organs, vessels and nerves there.

The plexus lies on the piriformis muscle on the posterolateral (back and side) wall of the true pelvis, posterior to the internal iliac vessels. L4 and L5 reach it as the lumbosacral trunk, and most branches leave through the greater sciatic foramen. Its position next to the rectum and in the path of the fetal head is why rectal cancer and childbirth can injure it (leg pain).

Roots run down the middle. Left column = posterior divisions: superior gluteal (L4–S1), inferior gluteal (L5–S2), and the common fibular part of the sciatic. Right column = anterior divisions: the tibial part of the sciatic. Between them: posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh (S2–S3) and pudendal (S2–S4). The fibular and tibial parts travel together as the sciatic nerve (L4–S3).

Medial view of the pelvic side wall. Find the thick lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) crossing down to join S1. The superior gluteal artery (the large unlabeled red loop) passes between the lumbosacral trunk and S1; the inferior gluteal artery passes between S2 and S3. The thin pelvic splanchnic nerves leave S2–S4 and run toward the rectum.

Colors: yellow = sympathetic, blue = parasympathetic, green = mixed (both), orange = somatic. Path: lumbar splanchnic nerves → superior hypogastric plexus (in front of L5, below the aortic split) → right and left hypogastric nerves → inferior hypogastric plexus beside the rectum, where they mix with the parasympathetic pelvic splanchnics. Don't confuse: sacral splanchnic nerves (from the sacral sympathetic trunk) are sympathetic; pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) are parasympathetic. Memory aid: parasympathetic = erection, sympathetic = ejaculation ('point and shoot').

Key: dashed lines = presynaptic (preganglionic) fibers; solid lines = postsynaptic (postganglionic) fibers. Blue area = organs supplied through cranial nerves (CN) III, VII, IX and X (X = vagus); green area = organs supplied by the sacral outflow. Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry the preganglionic fibers from S2–S4. They supply the gut from the left colic (splenic) flexure down (the diagonal border), plus the pelvic organs; the vagus covers the gut above that point. Their effects: contract the rectum and bladder walls to empty them, and cause erection.

pic.src: Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy 7e, Fig. I.48

slides.note: Stick diagram; arrows point the way blood flows. Aorta → common iliacs (at L4) → internal iliac (into the pelvis) and external iliac (becomes the femoral artery under the inguinal ligament). Just above the ligament the external iliac gives the inferior epigastric (which gives the cremasteric) and the deep circumflex iliac. @ = anastomosis with branches of the internal thoracic artery: inferior with superior epigastric, deep circumflex iliac with musculophrenic. These links can bypass a blocked aorta.

Unlabeled overview of the same arteries. Follow the aorta down: renal arteries to the sides, small paired lumbar arteries to the wall, the IMA leaving its front a little above the split, the split into common iliacs at L4, and the thin median sacral down the midline. Each common iliac splits into the internal iliac (dives into the pelvis) and the external iliac (runs along psoas). Near the inguinal ligament find the inferior epigastric going up and the deep circumflex iliac running laterally along the iliac crest.

The posterior division (PB, posterior branch; also called posterior trunk) feeds the wall and buttock, not the organs. Iliolumbar: up to iliacus, psoas and quadratus lumborum. Lateral sacrals: into the anterior sacral foramina. Superior gluteal: its largest branch and usual end; it passes between the lumbosacral trunk and S1, then leaves through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis.

Medial view of the pelvic side wall: front (external iliac) on the left, sacrum on the right. The internal iliac splits into the anterior trunk (cut short here) and the posterior trunk (= posterior division), whose three branches are in bold: iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal. The superior gluteal, its usual end, passes between the yellow nerve roots (lumbosacral trunk and S1). Don't confuse: the inferior gluteal is normally an end branch of the anterior division and leaves the pelvis below piriformis; only in some people does it come off the posterior division.

Colors: red arrows with black labels = both sexes; blue = male only; green = female only. @ = anastomosis: testicular artery with the artery to the ductus deferens; ovarian with uterine and vaginal; superior rectal (from the IMA) with middle and inferior rectal. The anterior division gives the organ branches and the obturator, then ends as the inferior gluteal (to the buttock) and the internal pudendal (to the perineum: inferior rectal, perineal, then dorsal and deep arteries of the penis or clitoris).

The obturator artery runs along the side wall to the obturator canal. In about 20% it arises from the inferior epigastric instead and descends past the femoral ring, so it can be cut during hernia repair. The superior vesical arteries come from the still-open start of the umbilical artery; the closed rest of it is the medial umbilical ligament.

View from above into the pelvis, front (pubic symphysis) at the bottom. A (women): water (the ureter, tan tube) passes under (inferior to) the bridge (the uterine artery) beside the cervix, near the lateral fornix of the vagina. When the uterine artery is clamped and tied during a hysterectomy, the ureter can be crushed, tied or cut with it. B (men): the bridge is the ductus deferens, which crosses over the ureter near the bladder.

pic.src: Gray's Anatomy for Students 3e, Fig. 5.12 (similar figure)

slides.note: Pelvic veins form plexuses around each organ. These connect with each other and drain mainly into the internal iliac vein. The rectal plexus is a portal–caval link: the superior rectal vein drains to the IMV (inferior mesenteric vein, portal system), while the middle and inferior rectal veins drain to the internal iliac vein (caval system). (m) = male only.

The pelvic plexuses connect, through the lateral sacral veins, with the internal vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus), whose veins have no valves. Coughing or straining can push pelvic blood, and cancer cells, backward into it. That is how prostate cancer reaches the lumbar vertebrae and even the brain, skipping the lungs.

qs.q: Which nerve supplies iliacus?
qs.why: Iliacus is supplied by the femoral nerve (L2–L4). Psoas major instead gets direct branches from the anterior rami of L1–L3.

qs.q: Where does psoas major insert, together with iliacus?
qs.why: Psoas major ends in a strong tendon on the lesser trochanter, and iliacus inserts on and just below the same tendon, so iliopsoas flexes the thigh.

qs.q: Which posterior abdominal wall muscle fixes the 12th rib during inspiration?
qs.why: Quadratus lumborum runs from the 12th rib to the iliac crest; it extends and laterally flexes the spine and holds the 12th rib down during inspiration.

qs.q: In the paravertebral gutter, where does the kidney lie relative to the posterior wall muscles?
opts: Lateral to psoas major, anterior to quadratus lumborum
Medial to psoas major, on the vertebral body
Anterior to psoas major, medial to the aorta
qs.why: The gutters beside the vertebrae hold the kidneys: each kidney sits lateral to psoas major and in front of quadratus lumborum, wrapped in perirenal fat and renal fascia.

qs.q: At what vertebral level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate into the common iliac arteries?
qs.why: The aorta enters at the aortic hiatus (T12) and splits at L4. L5 is where the common iliac veins join to form the IVC.

qs.q: Which aortic branches leave the lateral sides of the abdominal aorta?
qs.why: Lateral paired branches go to the urogenital and endocrine organs: renal, suprarenal and gonadal. The celiac, SMA and IMA leave the front; subcostal, inferior phrenic and lumbar leave the back-sides.

qs.q: How does the left renal vein reach the IVC?
opts: Drains first into the left common iliac vein
Crosses anterior to the aorta, just below the SMA
qs.why: The IVC lies right of the aorta, so the left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta, just below the SMA. The left lumbar veins are the ones that pass behind the aorta.

qs.q: Compression of the left renal vein between the SMA and aorta (nutcracker syndrome) can cause which scrotal finding?
qs.why: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, so back-up from the squeezed renal vein swells the veins around the left testis. The right testicular vein drains straight into the IVC.

qs.q: The lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior rami of which spinal nerves?
qs.why: The lumbar plexus is L1–L4 (often with a twig from T12). L5 joins part of L4 as the lumbosacral trunk, which belongs to the sacral plexus.

qs.q: The cremasteric reflex tests which spinal cord segments?
qs.why: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1–L2) supplies the cremaster, so stroking the upper inner thigh and seeing the testis lift tests L1–L2.

qs.q: Which lumbar plexus nerve leaves the medial border of psoas major?
qs.why: The obturator nerve runs deep and medial to psoas toward the true pelvis. The femoral nerve emerges laterally, in the groove between psoas and iliacus.

qs.q: Which nerve pierces psoas major and runs down its anterior surface?
qs.why: The genitofemoral nerve is the only lumbar plexus branch that pierces psoas; it lies on its front and splits into genital and femoral branches above the inguinal ligament.

qs.q: What kind of fibers do the lumbar splanchnic nerves carry?
qs.why: Lumbar splanchnic nerves carry preganglionic sympathetic fibers that synapse in ganglia of the plexuses around the aorta before reaching the pelvic organs.

qs.q: Why does extending the right thigh hurt in acute appendicitis (psoas sign)?
opts: It stretches psoas, which the inflamed appendix lies on
It contracts quadratus lumborum behind the cecum
It tightens the inguinal ligament over the appendix
It compresses the femoral nerve against the appendix
qs.why: Extending the thigh stretches psoas major. An inflamed organ resting on the muscle, like the appendix on the right, is pulled and hurts.

qs.q: Pus from a psoas abscess tracks down the psoas sheath and usually bulges where?
opts: In the upper thigh, below the inguinal ligament
In the lumbar region of the back
qs.why: The psoas sheath is a tube that passes deep to the inguinal ligament with the muscle, so pus (classically from TB of the lumbar spine) appears as a swelling in the upper thigh.

qs.q: In a thin person, against which vertebral body can the abdominal aorta be pressed at the umbilicus?
qs.why: The aorta lies on the L4 body at about the level of the umbilicus, just before it splits, so it can be compressed there to slow bleeding in the pelvis or legs.

qs.q: Which bones make up the pelvic girdle?
opts: Two hip bones and the L5 vertebra
Two hip bones, sacrum and coccyx
Two hip bones and two femurs
qs.why: The pelvic girdle is the two innominate (hip) bones plus the sacrum and coccyx. Ilium, ischium and pubis are the three parts of each hip bone, fused at puberty.

qs.q: Which iliac landmark anchors the lateral end of the inguinal ligament?
qs.why: The inguinal ligament runs from the ASIS (anterior superior iliac spine) to the pubic tubercle. The AIIS sits lower, just above the hip joint.

qs.q: Which landmark lies under the skin dimples of the lower back?
qs.why: The PSIS (posterior superior iliac spine) is the back end of the iliac crest and lies under the dimples of the low back.

qs.q: Where is bone marrow usually harvested from the pelvis?
qs.why: Marrow is drawn from the posterior part of the iliac crest, with the patient lying on the side.

qs.q: Which bony landmark is felt to guide a pudendal nerve block?
qs.why: The pudendal nerve crosses the sacrospinous ligament where it attaches to the ischial spine, so the spine is felt through the vagina and the needle goes just there.

qs.q: Which nerve supplies the front of the perineum and needs its own block, apart from a pudendal block?
qs.why: A pudendal block numbs most of the perineum, but the anterior part is supplied by the ilioinguinal nerve (L1), which is blocked separately.

qs.q: The ischiopubic ramus is the ramus of the ischium joined to which part of the pubis?
qs.why: The ramus of the ischium and the inferior ramus of the pubis together form the ischiopubic ramus, the lower rim of the obturator foramen.

qs.q: The linea terminalis is the arcuate line of the ilium plus which pubic ridge (with the pubic crest)?
qs.why: Arcuate line + pecten pubis + pubic crest = linea terminalis, the ridge that helps divide the true pelvis from the false pelvis.

qs.q: On an AP pelvis X-ray, which bone forms the upper rim of the obturator foramen?
qs.why: The superior pubic ramus forms the upper rim of the obturator foramen; the ischiopubic ramus forms its lower rim.

qs.q: What type of joint is the posterior part of the sacroiliac joint?
qs.why: The sacroiliac joint is mixed: synovial in front between the auricular surfaces, and a syndesmosis (bones held by ligament) behind, so it barely moves.

qs.q: Which ligament is the main weight-transferring ligament of the body?
qs.why: The interosseous part of the sacroiliac ligaments carries the weight of the trunk from the sacrum to the hip bones.

qs.q: Which ligament divides the sciatic foramen into greater and lesser sciatic foramina?
qs.why: The sacrospinous ligament (sacrum to ischial spine) has the greater sciatic foramen above it and the lesser one below it. The sacrotuberous ligament runs to the ischial tuberosity and closes the lesser foramen behind.

qs.q: Which structure forms the posterior part of the pelvic brim?
qs.why: The brim runs from the sacral promontory and sacral ala behind, along the linea terminalis, to the top of the pubic symphysis in front.

qs.q: Which bony landmarks form the lateral boundaries of the pelvic outlet?
qs.why: The diamond-shaped outlet has the pubic arch in front, the ischial tuberosities at the sides, and the sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx behind.

qs.q: Which organ lies in the true (lesser) pelvis?
qs.why: The true pelvis, below the pelvic brim, holds the bladder, reproductive organs and rectum. The cecum, appendix and ileocecal junction sit in the false pelvis, between the iliac wings.

qs.q: What forms the floor of the true pelvis?
qs.why: The true pelvis reaches down to the pelvic diaphragm (levator ani). The perineum lies below the pelvic diaphragm; the pelvic brim is its upper edge.

qs.q: What subpubic angle is typical of a female pelvis?
qs.why: The female pubic arch is wide (greater than 80°, fits between spread thumb and index finger); the male one is narrow (less than 70°).

qs.q: Structures passing through the obturator canal reach which region?
qs.why: The obturator nerve and vessels go through the obturator canal to the medial thigh. Structures under the inguinal ligament reach the front of the thigh.

qs.q: Which nerve leaves through the greater sciatic foramen and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen to reach the perineum?
qs.why: The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels exit through the greater sciatic foramen, hook around the ischial spine, then pass from the buttock through the lesser sciatic foramen into the perineum.

qs.q: A fall onto an extended leg most typically fractures which part of the pelvis?
qs.why: Landing on an extended leg drives the femoral head into the acetabulum. Front-to-back crushing in car crashes fractures the pubic rami instead.

qs.q: The sacral plexus is formed by the anterior rami of which spinal nerves?
qs.why: The sacral plexus is L4–S4; L4 and L5 reach it as the lumbosacral trunk. S2–S4 is the range of the pudendal and pelvic splanchnic nerves.

qs.q: Which nerve supplies gluteus maximus?
qs.why: The inferior gluteal nerve (L5–S2) supplies gluteus maximus. The superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae.

qs.q: Which nerve supplies the external anal sphincter and external urethral sphincter?
qs.why: The pudendal nerve (S2–S4) gives muscular branches to the perineal muscles and both external sphincters, and sensory branches to the external genitalia.

qs.q: The sciatic nerve arises from which roots?
qs.why: The sciatic nerve is L4–S3: its tibial part comes from the anterior divisions and its common fibular part from the posterior divisions. L4–S1 is the superior gluteal nerve.

qs.q: What fibers do the pelvic splanchnic nerves carry?
opts: Postganglionic sympathetic from the sacral trunk
qs.why: Pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic, from S2–S4. Don't mix them up with sacral splanchnic nerves, which are sympathetic.

qs.q: Where does the superior hypogastric plexus lie?
qs.why: The lumbar splanchnic nerves form the superior hypogastric plexus just below the aortic split, in front of L5. The inferior hypogastric plexus is the one beside the rectum.

qs.q: Which pelvic function is produced by sympathetic fibers?
qs.why: Sympathetic fibers contract the internal genital organs to produce ejaculation. Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnics cause erection and contract the bladder and rectum ('point and shoot').

qs.q: Pelvic splanchnic nerves supply the colon from which point downward?
qs.why: Pelvic splanchnics supply the gut from the left colic flexure down plus all pelvic organs; the vagus covers the gut above that point.

qs.q: The inferior epigastric artery anastomoses with which artery?
qs.why: The inferior epigastric (from the external iliac) meets the superior epigastric (from the internal thoracic). The deep circumflex iliac is the one that meets the musculophrenic.

qs.q: The external iliac artery becomes which artery after passing under the inguinal ligament?
qs.why: The external iliac runs along psoas and becomes the femoral artery under the inguinal ligament, giving the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac just above it.

qs.q: Which artery is a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery?
qs.why: The posterior division gives only the iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal arteries, which feed the wall and buttock rather than the organs.

qs.q: The superior gluteal artery usually passes between which two nerve structures?
qs.why: The superior gluteal artery runs between the lumbosacral trunk and S1, then leaves through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis. The inferior gluteal passes between S2 and S3.

qs.q: The anterior division of the internal iliac artery usually ends as which two arteries?
qs.why: After giving the organ branches and the obturator, the anterior division ends as the inferior gluteal (buttock) and internal pudendal (perineum).

qs.q: In about 20% of people, the obturator artery arises from which artery?
qs.why: An obturator artery from the inferior epigastric descends past the femoral ring, so it can be cut during hernia repair.

qs.q: The superior vesical arteries arise from the still-open part of which vessel?
qs.why: The start of the umbilical artery stays open and gives the superior vesical arteries; the closed remainder becomes the medial umbilical ligament.

qs.q: In females, which artery supplies the inferior bladder in place of a named inferior vesical artery?
qs.why: Females have no named inferior vesical artery; unnamed branches of the vaginal artery supply the inferior bladder.

qs.q: When the uterine artery is clamped during a hysterectomy, which structure passing beneath it can be injured?
qs.why: Water under the bridge: the ureter passes under the uterine artery beside the cervix, so it can be crushed, tied or cut when the artery is clamped.

qs.q: The superior rectal vein drains into which vessel?
qs.why: The superior rectal vein drains to the IMV (portal system), while the middle and inferior rectal veins drain to the internal iliac vein (caval system), making the rectal plexus a portal–caval link.

qs.q: Why can prostate cancer spread to the lumbar vertebrae without passing through the lungs?
opts: The internal iliac artery supplies the vertebral bodies
Prostatic veins drain into the portal system
Prostatic lymph drains directly into the IVC
Pelvic venous plexuses connect to the valveless vertebral venous plexus
qs.why: Pelvic plexuses connect with the internal vertebral venous (Batson) plexus, which has no valves, so straining pushes pelvic blood and tumor cells backward into the spine.

qs.q: Why can rectal cancer or childbirth cause leg pain?
opts: They injure the sacral plexus on the pelvic wall
They compress the femoral nerve inside psoas
They stretch the lumbar plexus over the pelvic brim
They block the external iliac artery
qs.why: The sacral plexus lies on the posterolateral wall of the true pelvis next to the rectum and in the path of the fetal head, so both can injure it.
